In America , ICE is now synonymous with the bumbling , thuggish secret service arm of a lunatic administration , aimed at reversing decades of multicultural immigration and run by unqualified bullies . It makes for a jarring contrast with the global festival of the Olympics , where the world comes together . The ICE division had previously been sent to the Games , apparently , but sending them now felt like a brutish warning as much as anything . After all , ICE is so dumb that it recently attempted to invade , uh , the Ecuadorian embassy in Minneapolis . <p> So , as Reuters reported , the left-wing mayor of Milan , Giuseppe Sala , called ICE " a militia that kills " in a radio interview , while Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani tried to reassure people by saying : " We 're not talking about the ( ICE personnel ) who were out on the streets of Minneapolis ... It 's not as if the ( Nazi ) SS are arriving . " Tajani apparently said this at a Holocaust memorial event , and it all must have been a huge relief for everyone involved , unless they have Twitter . <p> Geopolitical tensions are n't new , but America being this brand of geopolitical menace is . This is suddenly a world where flamboyantly questionable former FIFA president Sepp Blatter is advising nations to boycott this summer 's World Cup soccer matches in America , and where the current president of soccer 's international governing body , Gianni Infantino , has had to pander to U.S. President Donald Trump 's infantile whims with the nightmarish FIFA Peace Prize . Trump has packed loyalists onto the organizing committee for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles and when asked whether the IOC could replicate Infantino 's grovelling relationship with Trump , Coventry was almost a little too honest . " If we were n't seeing that good relationship , " she said , " I 'd be a little worried , right ? " <p> She should worry anyway . The IOC is replete with the kind of international sports grifter who thinks they 're too moral to work for FIFA , but the two organizations have gone on similar chases for money and global clout in the past 10 years , and have dragged the most remarkable sporting festivals on the planet to some dispiriting places as a result . <p> Now , Italy feels like the last stop before what could be a truly wretched Games in Los Angeles , before the scheduled 2028 U.S. presidential election . In the past month , Trump has stolen oil from Venezuela , threatened to invade Greenland , and his state forces killed two American citizens in Minnesota . God knows what will have happened to the U.S. in 2 1/2 years . <p> And MAGA , writ large , is an attack on the stated values of the Olympics : multinationalism , international co-operation , peace . For all of its own crony capitalism , the IOC has thrived in the post-war world of liberal democracy , and particularly since the Cold War ended . That relatively peaceful stretch , among other things , allowed for ludicrously charming Olympics in places where the IOC could become both comfortable and rich . Between 1992 and 2012 , as the Olympics really grew , the Games were held in six European cities ( Albertville , Barcelona , Lillehammer , Athens , Turin and London ) , two American cities ( Atlanta and Salt Lake City ) , then one trip each to Japan ( Nagano ) , Australia ( Sydney ) and Canada ( Vancouver ) . Oh , and the $44-billion ( U.S. ) extravaganza in Beijing , which was intended to be a signal of China 's rising power in the world . <p> But then came Sochi , at an estimated $51 billion , during which Russia ran the biggest performance-enhancing drug scandal in history and prepared to invade Ukraine . Which led back to Beijing in 2022 in part since Russia launched its assault on Crimea before the 2014 flame had stopped smoking , eliminating a Ukrainian bid , and the Sochi price tag scared off suitors such as Oslo and Stockholm . <p> Which helped lead , depending on how you look at it , to this moment in history , this Olympics , this place . Italy really is charming and the grace of the Games is that no matter how corrupt , how bankrupt , how cold , how suffocating , how disjointed or how authoritarian the orchestration of the Olympics , the humans always save it . The global sports system is full of venality and indignity , but the humans always save it . You can let the diving pool turn green or you can build an unfinished hockey rink that is the wrong size . You can go to Russia and China . It can get bad . <p> But now the central hub of the international rules-based order and chief money engine of the IOC is suddenly a dumb , rabid dog , and somehow that will intrude . Maybe it will feel like Paris somehow , romantic and sweet , a series of Olympic communities that become refuges from the world . Or maybe it will feel like taking refuge before a flood . <p> Read more <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Updated 6 sec ago <h> Curling Canada changed its ways ahead of the Milan Olympics . It hopes to have found the golden ingredients <p> A decade and a half ago , Curling Canada 's chief executive Nolan Thiessen played lead on the men 's team that won the world championship in Cortina d'Ampezzo , the Italian mountain town where curlers will vie for Olympic medals starting Wednesday . <p> Back then , each member played with a particular style : different starting positions , slides and releases . When someone 's in-turn curled more than their out-turn , they did n't try to fix that . They just put their brooms to work . <p> From Thiessen 's day until quite recently , Canadian curlers more or less did their own thing . That 's changed since Scottish import David Murdoch arrived in 2023 to lead Canada 's high-performance program and usher in a more modern era of technical training , video analysis and , crucially , getting everyone to deliver the rock the same way . <p> When everyone uses the same body and stone position , from the hack through the initial slide out , shots are more predictable and it becomes easier to sweep , read the ice and understand the line . Curlers learn from every shot , increasing the probability of making the next one . <p> " It 's definitely an improvement for us as a nation , and it will continue to pay dividends , " Thiessen says . <p> Getting here was n't easy . <p> Canada 's historic dominance internationally and highly competitive national scene led to resistance of the newest techniques and trends , even while European and Asian nations used them to beat Canadians . <p> " You get punched in the mouth and you fight back , " Thiessen adds , " and that 's really what we 're doing . " <p> Murdoch , a multiple world and Olympic medallist , has helped Canadian curlers buy in to change . <p> Many top countries have curling centres where national teams benefit from structured daily high-level training , and Murdoch has adapted that to Canada 's vast geography and competitive landscape . That includes : more training camps early in the season ; more access to national coaches and resources ; and support for individual team coaches , wherever they 're located , with development plans backed by competition data . <p> It 's an environment of constant learning all the way to the Olympics , when it matters most . As Murdoch puts it : " It 's easy to say we won or we lost a competition , but actually what did we learn ? " <p> Canada 's three teams will travel to Italy in hopes of reaping the benefits of a series of changes , big and small . <p> Five-time national champion Rachel Homan passed on this week 's Scotties Tournament of Hearts to rest up for the Olympics . Two days after Sunday 's Canadian final in Mississauga , Homan 's team will fly to a staging camp in Brunico , Italy . <p> And when they arrive in the athletes village outside Cortina , they 'll have mattress toppers ( the kind used by international cyclists ) to upgrade their beds and help with rest and recovery through the tournament . <p> Technical training , detailed preparation and a consistent shot are what it takes to become an Olympic champion in this era . <p> " There is no circumventing that , " Murdoch says . " The key to high-level performance teams is just real consistency : the same slide , same release , same delivery , same communications , very clear strategies . So when you tie that all together , that 's an Olympic gold medal-winning team . " <p> The first Canadians to compete will be the married duo of Jocelyn Peterman and Brett Gallant in mixed doubles , which starts Wednesday , two days before the opening ceremony . Peterman finished fifth at the 2022 Beijing Games with skip Jennifer Jones , while Gallant was third with Brad Gushue 's rink . After mixed doubles , Gallant will go on to compete with Brad Jacobs ' team . <p> Peterman says one key change that all Canadian teams have adopted -- moving the rock to the centre of the hack -- will help on the international stage even if it has proven to be a tricky adjustment . <p> " Honestly , it feels a little bit uncomfortable when you 're first setting up , " she says . " We 're a bit more squished . <p> " We have to be very intentional about where we start the rock . As soon as we start the rock in the right spot and we push forward , our body comes right behind the rock and there 's no moving parts . There 's no kind of room for error in terms of lateral movement , and that 's what we 're looking to deliver : the rock on an , ideally , perfectly straight line . " <p> That 's something she has seen in real time in training sessions with Scott Pfeifer , Canada 's mixed doubles coach , who sets up laser lines on the ice and records shots from three angles . That lets Peterman and Gallant reconcile how they feel with what they see and make any corrections . <p> Peterman 's women 's team , skipped by Kaitlyn Lawes , adopted the change three years ago , while Gallant 's foursome switched last year . Curlers spend years fine-tuning , so there 's a learning curve . <p> " There 's a period of time where you feel a bit naked out there and you 're like : I think I know where this is going , but it 's not second nature yet and I still have to focus on it , " Gallant says . <p> He adds that change was necessary : " Canadian curling athletes have had to adopt a growth mindset over the last four , six , 10 years because the world has gotten so talented and so deep . We 've had to start looking for ways to get one per cent better . " <p> Curling is among Canada 's oldest sports dating to 1807 , long before Confederation , when Scottish immigrants started a club in Montreal . Globally , the sport has expanded from the six founders of World Curling 60 years ago to 76 countries today . It was part of the first Winter Olympics in 1924 and , after a lengthy hiatus , returned to the Olympic menu in 1998 . <p> Canada has n't won Olympic gold in the men 's or women 's event since a 2014 sweep by Jacobs and Jennifer Jones in Sochi , Russia . The last mixed doubles medal was gold in its Olympic debut in 2018 . <p> Jacobs , back for another shot , calls the 2014 Games " the hardest bonspiel ever . Ski jumping is physics : the more surface area , the further you glide ; the stiffer the suit material , the more it penetrates through the wind . There are rules about how baggy a suit can be : jumpers are now measured all over with 3D scanners , so every inch matters . And the crotch is right out front , so as so many erectile dysfunction ads have said , enhancing your manhood enhances your performance . One study showed a two-centimetre change in a suit 's circumference could increase a jump length by an astonishing 5.8 metres . <p> So it 's both the equipment , and what you do with it . Penis-packing is a peculiar type of indignity for a sport , and it might even drive away future athletes . After all , who wants to belong to a club that would have you as a member ? <p> But why did the penis frenzy , as Bild called it back in January in a headline , erupt now ? Bild reported the alleged penis injections during the 4 Hills , a venerable German-Austrian ski jumping competition that has been taking place since 1953 ; the tabloid quoted a doctor named Kamran Karim as saying : " It is possible to achieve a temporary , visual thickening of the penis by injecting paraffin or hyaluronic acid . " <p> But there is no hard evidence of this actually happening . So why is it springing up now , in the sport the Germans call skispringen ? <p> Well , writing about penises is probably a fun way to enliven an annual ski jumping competition , especially if the central pillar of the piece happens to be plausible , if not precisely firm . And here at the Olympics , the British media were thrilled to throw a penis question into the mix , and WADA seemed happy enough to answer any question that did n't involve its bigger problems . Such as , say , the fact that the Trump administration has decided not to pay its annual dues until WADA addresses its alleged cover-up of 23 positive test cases in the Chinese swim program in 2021 . <p> And for the record , WADA absolutely appeared to cover up the doping cases , and late last year , the German public broadcaster ARD cited internal WADA documents that referred to Operation Puncture , which was described as an effort to expose whistleblowers on the Chinese swim scandal . The Trump administration never gets anything right , but this issue might be the closest thing : the Chinese doping case involves real stakes , on a globally significant scale . WADA is now talking about taking away testing from each individual nation , because of the prospect of nationalistic corruption of the system . The Chinese doping case , like Russian state-sponsored doping before it , has shaken the pillars of the global anti-doping system . <p> On the other hand , some ski jumpers exaggerate their junk in ways we know about -- and it was the usually respectable Norwegians , imagine -- and might swell their genitalia in ways most people have never imagined . Does the sport need a biological passport for penises , checking periodically to make sure they stay the same size ? Is penis size now a competitive advantage , unlike in , say , pole vault ? <p> Citius , altius , fortius , penis . THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck <p> DD Toronto Star <p> TORONTO - Olympic officials made the right call in postponing the Canada-Finland women 's hockey game on Thursday after several players on the Finnish team came down with norovirus , doctors say . <p> " This is the sprinter of viruses . This thing moves fast , " said Dr. Nitin Mohan , a physician and epidemiologist at Western University in London , Ont . <p> " ( Officials ) did a great job to suspend the game , which likely prevented a spread to the Canadian team , " he said . <p> Here are a few things to know about norovirus . <p> WHAT IS NOROVIRUS ? <p> Norovirus is a common cause of gastrointestinal illness usually characterized by the sudden onset of vomiting and/or diarrhea . People often call it " stomach flu . " <p> " The best name from my perspective is the Brits call it ' winter vomiting disease , ' " said Dr. Allison McGeer , an infectious disease specialist at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto . <p> HOW LONG DOES IT LAST ? <p> Most people have active gastrointestinal symptoms for 24 to 36 hours , McGeer said . In some cases it can last 48 hours . <p> " You get sudden onset of vomiting and/or diarrhea . And then , you know , you do n't leave the bathroom for six hours . And then it gets better . And then by the next day , you do n't have diarrhea or vomiting anymore . You just feel like you 've been hit by a truck , " she said . <p> " And the day after that , you 're pretty much back to normal , " although fatigue can linger , McGeer said . <p> HOW DO PEOPLE GET INFECTED ? <p> Norovirus is very contagious . <p> It 's typically found in traces of fecal matter and spreads through contact with an infected person , through food handled by an infected person or touching contaminated surfaces . <p> People can also get it from aerosols released in the air when an infected person is vomiting , both Mohan and McGeer said . <p> Norovirus outbreaks are common in daycares , long-term care homes and anywhere people are living together in close contact with each other . <p> " The Olympics setting is almost ideal for the virus to spread -- folks in close contact , communal eating , ( a ) highly stressful environment ( so ) your immune system is suppressed , " Mohan said . <p> " It 's not all too surprising for anyone in our field that this has happened . Quite frankly , I 'm surprised it does n't happen more often . " <p> IS THERE TREATMENT FOR NOROVIRUS ? <p> No . The most important thing people can do is to drink fluids because the vomiting and diarrhea make them dehydrated . <p> There 's not much else people can do except to rest , the doctors said . <p> For the vast majority of people , norovirus is " horrible when you get it , but it will pass , " Mohan said . <p> McGeer said she worries about severe dehydration in very small children , people who are immunocompromised and older frail people . <p> In some cases , people suffering from severe hydration may need to go to the emergency department to get IV fluids , she said . <p> In very rare cases , people who are very frail can die because the dehydration disrupts their salt balance , which in turn can lead to heart problems . <p> But that 's " really uncommon , " she said . <p> HOW CAN PEOPLE PREVENT NOROVIRUS FROM SPREADING ? <p> Frequent handwashing with soap and water is critical , both Mohan and McGeer said . <p> Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are n't as effective for norovirus as they are with other viruses , but can still have some benefit . <p> Using bleach to clean surfaces is also important . <p> It 's also vital to isolate people with norovirus quickly to prevent spread to others , which is what the Finnish women 's hockey team did , Mohan said . <p> " Kudos to the athletes for informing the right individuals to ensure that the correct protocols had been taking place , " he said . <p> " I think this is sort of a great learning opportunity for the broader public to just be aware of how quickly this virus can spread . " <p> This report by The Canadian Press was first published Feb. 6 , 2026 . <p> Canadian Press health coverage receives support through a partnership with the Canadian Medical Association . The cancellation of the consumer carbon tax made polluting cheaper , while the lengthy " pause " of the electric vehicle rebate made EVs more expensive . There is no more federal government money for green home renovations , but there are billions of dollars for new pipelines and liquid natural gas ( LNG ) export projects . Decades of fossil fuel production are being locked in , while renewable energy construction has sputtered . <p> If you read the news with an eye for the climate , 2025 was a bad year . <p> But all this denial and neglect risks drowning out a different story , one of marked progress in efforts to deal with climate change virtually everywhere else in the world . Key indicators show @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ presage a peak to global emissions . <p> While it may be hard for some to believe , last year was actually a good year on the climate front , experts say . And we 'd be able to see it , if we 'd only look past our immediate surroundings . <p> " North America is uniquely decelerating in a world where everything else is accelerating , " said Daan Walter , principal at the U.K.-based energy think-tank Ember . " If you would look at the world and hold your hand over the United States , you would see the acceleration very clearly . " <p> A Chinese worker works on a solar panel project . Thanks to a dramatic drop in the cost of solar panels and batteries , countries on every continent are installing record amounts of renewables , which overtook coal to become the top source of electricity worldwide in 2025 . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> A record number of EVs were also sold last year , the total jumping 20 per cent over 2024 . Again , this is largely thanks to the incredible amount of wind and solar generation being built . <p> In the past 12 months , China installed so much renewable power that it has stopped the rise in its use of coal and burned less than it did the previous year -- for the first time in more than 50 years ( outside of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that clean electricity , China has been electrifying road transport at an astonishing rate . @@134249833 <h> Want to mitigate overland flood risk ? Check upstream as well as downstream <p> By David Gambrill February 9 , 2026 Last updated on February 9 , 2026 <p> 4 min read <p> Plus Icon Image <p> B.C. documentary filmmaker Daniel Pierce has focused his lens on how deforestation , combined with climate change , elevates the risk of flood damage in the province 's river basins . <p> Pierce appeared by video link at the CatIQ Connect claims conference in Toronto last Tuesday . He spoke about his 25-minute documentary , Trouble in the Headwaters , which premiered in Victoria , B.C. , in June 2025 . <p> Presented by The Narwhal , the film analyzes root causes behind the 2018 floods in Grand Forks , B.C. , where more than 100 families were displaced and an estimated $38 million in damage was caused to more than 500 buildings in the flooded area . <p> Much of the damage was not eligible for insurance coverage , since policy deductibles for overland flood ranged between $2,000 and $100,000 , brokers reported to Canadian Underwriter at the time . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of forest hydrology at the University of British Columbia . Alila published a controversial academic research paper in 2009 claiming , in very basic terms : " While large floods may not appear to increase much in magnitude due to loss of tree cover , they may occur more frequently as a result of forest harvesting or deforestation . " <p> Pierce 's film features Alila and specifically analyzes the impact of clear-cut logging on flooding in the Kettle River watershed in the Grand Forks area . <p> " When the 2018 flood happened ... reports started to arise that this was n't just a climate event ; it was n't just about the rain and the snow , " Pierce told property and casualty insurance professionals via video link to the conference . " There was actually more going on in the landscape upstream from Grand Forks , in the broader Kettle River basin . <p> " A lot of people were saying that this was connected to clearcut logging all throughout the headwaters of the Kettle , and so I decided to shift my focus as a journalist @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the ground . " <p> Pierce cited images in his film of a 600-hectare logging clearcut in the area , which he said was supposed to be limited by regulation to 40 hectares . Since the 1980s , he noted , time lapse photography by Google Maps showed a significant amount of deforestation happening in areas of the basin . This , Alila claims in his research , increases the frequency of extreme flooding events attributed to climate change . <p> " What Dr. Alila 's research has really revealed is that ... when all the other climate factors remain the same , that forest cover does a ton of work in lowering the risk and lowering the amount of runoff that comes down into stream channels , " Pierce told CatIQ delegates . " And when you remove that forest cover ... that natural mechanism or reducing flood risk is lost , and the water comes pouring off the hillsides all at once . " <p> Depending on the nature of the watershed , clearcut logging can increase the frequency of floods by anywhere between five and 18 times @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That means structures we designed to withstand a 100-year flood are now in a lot of danger , and are no longer going to be sufficient in the long run , because that 100-year flood could now become a 10-year flood or a five-year flood . " <p> Pierce cited the example of Abbotsford , B.C. , a city of more than 150,000 people in the province 's Fraser Valley . Severe flooding from an atmospheric river in 2021 caused more than $670 million in insured damage in the area , as Insurance Bureau of Canada reported last year . <p> Abbotsford flooded again in 2024 , and yet again in December 2025 . The 2025 flooding , caused by an atmospheric river , resulted in estimated insured damage of $90 million . <p> Pierce noted the 2021 floods in Abbotsford led to a " managed retreat , " including the city buying out 100 properties with a backing of $50 million . In Spring 2024 , the province introduced a 10-year plan for flood risk mitigation in the area , but a Vancouver Sun report noted the plan had @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no timelines . " <p> Pierce said insurers tend to deal with the natural disasters caused downstream . But , in addition to climate change , they should be considering how deforestation upstream can be contributing to the frequency of flood events . <p> " The most important thing is that , if we 're going to be making millions -- if not billions -- of dollars of investments in the downstream to mitigate flood risk , we must synchronize our policies in the upstream to make sure we 're not continuing to make the problem worse , " Pierce said . " We should also be doing restoration and careful stewardship and bringing back the intact forest covering the upstream , so that we can lower that risk over time . <p> " That is a generational project that needs to be committed to in the long haul . @@134249834 <h> For insurers , climate change is just the tip of the iceberg <p> Insurance companies ' warnings are making true believers of home insurance policyholders , who face higher prices and shrinking coverage <p> By Anushka Yadav , Local Journalism Initiative Reporter , The Pointer ( Courtesy of The Canadian Press ) February 9 , 2026 Last updated on February 9 , 2026 <p> 9 min read <p> Plus Icon Image <p> iStock.com/Dragon Claws <p> With global temperature rising and extreme weather becoming the new normal , ballooning insurance premiums and shrinking coverage are hitting Canadians hard . Instead , they are doing the opposite ; quietly rewriting the rules of risk as extreme weather becomes more frequent , more destructive and more expensive . <p> In 2025 , the planet was battered by 55 billion-dollar weather catastrophes marked by the most expensive wildfire ever recorded , four catastrophic floods and storms , along with the sixth-deadliest heat wave in history , each of which took at least 1,000 lives . <p> In Canada , insured losses from severe weather including ice storms , wildfires and flooding , exceeded $2.4 billion , according to Catastrophe Indices and Quantification Inc . ( CatIQ ) . This made 2025 the tenth costliest year on record for severe weather-related insured losses in Canada . <p> Last year 's late-March ice storm in Ontario and Quebec contributed heavily to losses ( $490 million ) but this year , Ontario experienced a record-breaking winter storm earlier . On @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of snow in parts of the Greater Toronto Area with Toronto Pearson Airport recording its snowiest day in 88 years with 46.2 centimetres , though the insured losses are still unknown . <p> But 2024 remains historic , with insured damage reaching a record $9.4 billion ( 12 times the annual average from 2001 to 2010 ) , the costliest year in Canadian history for severe weather losses . <p> Much of that cost is ultimately passed on to homeowners through higher premiums , reduced coverage or outright exclusions . <p> In the Region of Peel , many areas in Mississauga , like Lisgar , Applewood Acres and Rathwood where residents say " flooding has become a way of life " , have borne the brunt , with insurance providers reportedly cancelling flood coverage , leaving homeowners fully responsible for any future flood damage . <p> Ward 3 Rathwood neighbourhood resident Karri Siemms says her home has flooded three times , once in 2013 and twice in 2024 . <p> " Our home insurance premiums are now double what they should be for a comparable property , " Siemms told @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ month for home insurance alone . " <p> For her family , switching insurers is unfortunately not an option . <p> " Other insurance companies will not even provide a quote . " <p> Feltmate likens the trend to a baseball player suddenly hitting five times as many home runs after taking steroids . <p> " You ca n't attribute any single home run to the steroids . @@134264765 <h> Behold , the chart of the century , Canadian edition <p> When economist Mark Perry unveiled a graph in 2016 showing where inflation was lurking in the U.S. economy , it was quickly tagged as a candidate for " chart of the century . " <p> The chart , which simply broke down U.S. inflation rates by category , is now famous in financial circles for what it depicts about globalization , the benefits of international competition , and what 's at stake now that free trade is being unwound and protectionist policy is remaking the world order . <p> A Canadian version of the chart is no less fascinating . Over the past 25-plus years , inflation has been hottest in non-tradeable segments , including education and shelter , while tradeable goods have mostly come down in price , some dramatically so , such as electronics . <p> " We 've had a period where globalization helped lower inflation for most tradeable goods and thus lifted the purchasing power of most households , " said Pedro Antunes , chief economist at Signal49 Research , formerly The Conference Board @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ make it more challenging for the Bank of Canada and other central banks to keep inflation at target . " <p> One of the reasons this chart , and its updated versions , have been making the rounds for a decade now is because they tell so many different stories . Here are some of the big ones packed into the Canadian edition . <h> Free trade = cheap stuff <p> As barriers to international trade have steadily come down over the past few decades , the effect on consumer prices has been unmistakable . <p> Things like furniture , clothing and toys cost about as much , or less , than they did at the turn of the century , according to Statistics Canada 's pricing data . ( While your favourite pair of jeans may have gone up over time , the price tags on these categories overall have stayed steady . ) <p> For open economies like Canada 's , globalization " has imparted a steady disinflationary bias , " as production shifted to lower-cost producers and countries with cheaper labour , Mark Carney said in a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ England . <p> The effect is most dramatic when it comes to items like televisions , computers and other electronic devices , which have declined on the order of 85 to 90 per cent , after accounting for how technology has advanced over the years . A big-screen TV would have cost you much more than $1,000 in the early-2000s , for example . These days , you can pick up a high-definition smart TV that size for as little as $300 . Statistics Canada further adjusts the sticker-price decline to account for the vast improvement in quality , to ensure they are comparing apples to apples . <p> Vehicle prices are also adjusted for quality improvements . But categories like clothing have seen prices decline on an absolute basis . <h> Free trade ? cheap services <p> The chart clearly shows what has been putting pressure on Canadian household budgets over the years . Costs in the service industries , like education and health care , have dramatically outpaced overall inflation . Same with shelter . <p> There are some common elements here . These industries are not subject @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ labour component , such that rising wages drive prices up . And in some cases , the cost of regulation contributes to inflation , as well . <p> Food is a bit of an outlier . While labour costs play a role , food is largely an imported good that has seen major price increases in Canada . There is plenty to blame -- climate change and extreme weather , lack of competition , heavy transportation costs , and deficiencies in the Canadian supply chain among them . <p> In a way , economic integration has helped dull the impact of high prices for things like food and education , which have been partially offset by the falling cost of trade-sensitive goods . <h> The globalization backlash <p> Since economic integration has helped dampen inflation in some respects , the protectionist forces gaining strength today risk sending the prices of goods higher in the years ahead . <p> Tariffs are inflationary . Economist Paul Krugman recently calculated on his blog that tariffs on U.S. imports are responsible for about 0.8 percentage points of U.S. inflation today . And that 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to flow into the country duty-free under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement . <p> Brexit may serve as a cautionary example . The exit of the United Kingdom from the European Union in 2020 caused food prices to rise by about 6 per cent over the following two years , according to a pair of studies . <h> Wages outpaced prices <p> Contrary to popular belief , Canadian wages have increased at a faster pace than inflation since the end of 1999 . <p> This has become a heated issue in Canada , with many consumers feeling like the cost of living has gotten steadily worse , at the same time as economists point out that the average consumer is better off , with a higher income even after accounting for inflation . <p> Part of the discrepancy may lie in the income gap . Affordability issues are felt more acutely by those lower on the income scale , said Claire Fan , senior economist at Royal Bank of Canada . " Those that earn lower wages are also the ones that tend to be the most impacted by rising inflation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of inflation <p> Even after accounting for the inflation crisis of 2021-23 , prices overall have tracked pretty close to target . Since the start of the 2000s , overall Canadian inflation amounted to about 76 per cent , which is only about 10 percentage points higher than it would have been if the Consumer Price Index rose by the 2-per-cent annual target each and every year . <p> The takeaway is that even modest inflation can have a major impact when it accumulates over many years . This is an especially important lesson for retirees , who generally need to plan for about 25 years of post-career finances , says Doug Porter , Bank of Montreal chief economist . <p> " Even if the Bank of Canada is largely successful in hitting its inflation target over the next 25 years , you 're going to have to accept that prices could rise by 70 per cent or more over that period . "

Adjusted EBITDA margin is adjusted EBITDA as a proportion of revenue . Western uses adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA margin as benchmark measurements of our own operating results and as benchmarks relative to our competitors . We consider adjusted EBITDA to be a meaningful supplement to operating income as a performance measure primarily because amortization expense , impairment adjustments and changes in the fair value of biological assets are non-cash costs , and vary widely from company to company in a manner that we consider largely independent of the underlying cost efficiency of their operating facilities . Further , the inclusion of operating restructuring items which are unpredictable in nature and timing may make comparisons of our operating results between periods more difficult . We also believe adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA margin are commonly used by securities analysts , investors and other interested parties to evaluate our financial performance . <p> Adjusted EBITDA does not represent cash generated from operations as defined by IFRS and it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Furthermore , adjusted EBITDA does not reflect the impact of certain items that affect our net income . Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA margin are not measures of financial performance under IFRS , and should not be considered as alternatives to measures of performance under IFRS . Moreover , because all companies do not calculate adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA margin in the same manner , these measures as calculated by Western may differ from similar measures calculated by other companies . A reconciliation between the **27;1992;TOOLONG ; s net income as reported in accordance with IFRS and adjusted EBITDA is included in this press release . <p> Also in this press release management may use key performance indicators such as net debt , net debt to capitalization , and current assets to current liabilities . @@134265112 <p> A new study conducted at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research ( PIK ) shows that grassland-based grazing systems - currently covering a third of the Earth 's surface and representing the world 's largest production system - will see a severe contraction as global temperatures rise . Depending on the scenario analysed , 36-50 percent of the land with suitable climatic conditions for grazing today will experience a loss of viability by 2100 , affecting more than 100 million pastoralists and up to 1.6 billion grazing animals . <p> The study , published in the scientific journal PNAS , identifies a ' safe climatic space ' for cattle , sheep and goat grazing . To date , these agricultural systems have thrived within certain ranges of temperature ( from -3 to 29 ? C ) , rainfall ( between 50 and 2627 millimetres per year ) , humidity ( from 39 to 67 percent ) and wind speeds ( between 1 and 6 metres per second ) . <p> " Climate change will shift and significantly contract these spaces globally , leaving fewer spaces for animals to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in countries that already experience hunger , economic and political instability , and higher levels of gender inequity , " commented lead author Chaohui Li , PIK researcher at the time the study was conducted and now with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center . <p> " Grassland-based grazing is highly dependent on the environment , including things like temperature , humidity , and water availability . What we see is that climate change is going to reduce the spaces in which grazing can thrive , fundamentally challenging farming practices that have existed for centuries , " commented Maximilian Kotz , another of the study 's coauthors and researcher at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center and PIK . <h> Africa a hotspot for impacts on grazing <p> The authors highlight that Africa will be particularly vulnerable . Grasslands in Africa could reduce by 16 percent in a low emissions scenario , or up to 65 percent in a future in which fossil fuels continue to expand , as temperatures on the continent already sit at the upper end of the safe climatic space identified as suitable for grazing . <p> As temperatures rise @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Ethiopian highlands , the East African Rift Valley , the Kalahari Basin , and the Congo Basin will shift southward . Because the African landmass terminates at the Southern Ocean , these suitable temperature belts would eventually extend beyond the continent 's edge , resulting in a loss of viable grazing land . <p> " This shift away from what we 're identifying as the safe climatic space really challenges the efficacy of adaptation strategies that have been used in places such as Africa in times of hardship , such as switching species or migrating herds . The changes are just too big for that , " said Prajal Pradhan , assistant professor of the University of Groningen , PIK researcher and a coauthor of the study . <p> " Reducing emissions by rapidly moving away from fossil fuels is the best strategy we have to minimise these potentially existential damages for livestock farming , " Li concluded . <p> This article has been republished from the following materials . Note : material may have been edited for length and content . @@134265417 <h> How a whole brain perspective could reshape the global economy . <h> Key points <p> Since the COVID-19 pandemic , there has been a global shift in the way we talk about brain health . <p> At the World Economic Forum in Davos , an international nonmedical spotlight shone on brain health . <p> More than one in three people are affected by neurological conditions worldwide . <p> Is there something you did n't like as a kid that you really love now ? Maybe it 's onions , spicy food , or running . <p> For me , it was anything to do with brains . In medical school , the speciality I disliked the most was neurology . I was interested in the neurological symptoms that I read about in textbooks and that patients described to me , but the science and teaching of brain function and the diseases associated with it left me running for the canteen . To me , there was already a mismatch ; the complexity of what people were experiencing felt oversimplified by just having to learn the area of the brain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state the prescription required . ( And the neurologists were very strict , which did n't help ! ) <p> Since being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2014 , I 've done a full 180 on brain science , and now it 's something that endlessly fascinates me . Personal experience always reframes health with a new lens , but when it comes to anything " neuro , " it 's become more than that for me . The more I learned about brain health , the more I realised how integral our brain is to every single aspect of our inner and outer lives . From emotional health to gut health and creativity , productivity , and happiness , my jaw was on the ground when I realised that caring for our brains was at the core of improving our lives . <p> Since the COVID-19 pandemic , there has been a global shift in the way we talk about brain health . @@134298166 <p> Bayati , a PhD candidate in the department of Earth , ocean and atmospheric sciences , was initially interested in how nature sustains us and its complexity as both " kind and brutal " -- kind because of the resources it provides , but brutal in the floods and disasters that can follow . The importance of nature to human life led him to study water resources management . <p> " Water security is one of the pillars of security in any country , " said Bayati in an interview with The Ubyssey . Water is tied to food systems and economic stability . This means that predicting river flows is not only about safety , but about understanding water 's behaviour for our own use . <p> Deep learning is being used more and more in rainfall-run-off modelling -- the process of predicting how much water will flow in rivers , based on hydrological data and simulations of the water cycle . In their new paper , however , Bayati and his co-authors note that while models like Long Short-Term Memory ( LSTM ) networks can achieve great @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ learn statistical patterns , not tangible hydrologic mechanisms , which raises doubts about whether their internal logic is reliable . <p> Accuracy and reliability are n't the same thing . Bayati compares the difference to studying for an exam : if you memorize the exact parts that appear on the test , you might do well ( accuracy ) -- but if you change the questions to require deeper understanding and application , you flunk ( a lack of reliability ) . For water forecasting , the " exam " is complicated by climate change , heat waves and unfamiliar extremes . <p> This problem ( of models not being able to pass the harder exam ) is rooted in how most machine learning works : deep learning models are often described as " black boxes , " meaning we can see what goes in and what comes out , but not what 's happening in the middle . <p> In a river flow model , the inputs are environmental data . Bayati 's paper considered daily precipitation ( rainfall/snowfall ) , temperature , evaporation , and observed streamflow from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ North America . The output is a river flow prediction . But if the model is a black box , Bayati said you ca n't really tell how it made that prediction -- or whether it 's doing it in a way that makes physical sense . " We can not tell if it is ... just memorizing . " <p> To address this problem and test whether these " high-performing " models are functionally realistic ( meaning their internal behaviours and processes align with defensible physical mechanisms ) , the team used an Explainable AI ( XAI ) framework . XAI essentially " opens this black box " to peek inside and check whether a model that looks accurate on paper is actually using sensible relationships . <p> The team did n't focus on places where the model performed badly ; the real question was whether high accuracy came from the right reasoning . <p> The answer was no . Across the 672 catchments they evaluated , Bayati said they " saw bad reasoning everywhere . " <p> In rain-dominated basins like those on the West Coast , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Short-term temperature rises increased simulated streamflow , even though Bayati said , " temperature should n't impact river flow in rain-dominated regions . " <p> Similarly , in snow-dominated regions , the model tended to misattribute the cause of snowmelt-related flow . Simply put , the model saw that increased evaporation and river flow tended to co-occur , which it interpreted as a causal relationship -- that an increase in evaporation causes an increase in river flow . The model missed the third variable , temperature , which is what actually causes an increase in both evaporation and river flow . <p> The model confused " things that happen together " with " things that cause each other . " This is something every research student knows to be faulty -- correlation is not causation . But this fault poses risks when forecasting under new climate conditions . The authors argue that this correlation-driven learning can undermine accuracy under weather extremes and both short- and long-term climatic shifts . <p> A natural followup is : if we know the physics , why not add them in ? The paper does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to add constraints , discouraging models from violating relationships that could never happen physically . But while these physics-backed models do exist , they 're not widely used , for two reasons . <p> First , convenience : pure deep learning is much easier to train and deploy . Second , trust : physics-informed methods are still new in some subfields , including hydrology , and some researchers remain unconvinced they can deliver on what they promise -- though Bayati said the literature is growing and he himself is working on some physics-informed model followup studies . <p> In a climate that 's becoming less predictable and pushing water systems into new conditions -- Vancouver is on track for its first snow-free winter since 1982 , according to Environment Canada -- the stakes are rising ; and models ' predictions will need to be able to hold as the rules change as well . " Maybe in the future , they 'll be much better . @@134302270 <p> Complimenting others regularly can make you less critical of yourself as the habit turns inward . <p> Source : Lindsey Godwin/Dall-E/Used with permission <p> This week , I was standing in line at a coffee shop when I noticed the woman in front of me wearing the most unapologetically joyful pair of yellow boots . The kind of yellow that skips right past muted mustard and lands on full sunflower , like a little wink of summer on a dreary winter day . <p> As most of us would , I almost kept the thought to myself . We notice something lovely and swallow it . Instead , I heard myself say , " I just have to tell you , those boots are fantastic . " <p> She turned around , startled for half a second , and then her whole face shifted . She lit up with a real smile , the kind that starts in the eyes and spreads from cheek to cheek . She laughed and said , " I was n't sure if I could pull them off . " <p> " You absolutely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it . We both ordered our drinks and went on with our days , yet the energy in that small square of space had changed , all in less than 10 seconds . <p> Why This Tiny Thing Matters More Than We Think <p> There 's solid research behind what happened in that coffee line . <p> In a 2021 study , Zhao and Epley found that people consistently underestimate how good it feels to receive a compliment . The givers worry they 'll come off awkward or intrusive , but the receivers report feeling significantly more uplifted than the givers predicted . Our hesitation is usually based on faulty assumptions . We convince ourselves it will be awkward , or that it wo n't matter much , and we 're usually wrong . <p> There is also a body of research in positive psychology showing that small acts of kindness increase well-being for the person performing them . Sonja Lyubomirsky and her colleagues have found that intentional acts of kindness can boost happiness and life satisfaction when practiced consistently ( 2013 ) . What I love about this : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nonprofit , a five-year plan , or a perfectly curated gratitude journal . It asks us to pay attention and say something out loud . <p> There is something almost mischievous about how simple it is . <p> Why We Do n't Do It <p> If this is so powerful , why do we hesitate ? <p> Part of it is social anxiety . We do n't want to intrude or be misunderstood . Many of us , especially women , have learned to be cautious about how we engage strangers . There 's a broader cultural script running underneath as well . We 've been trained to ' see something , say something ' when something looks wrong . No one ever encouraged us to do the same when something looks good . <p> And yet , we all know what it feels like to be authentically seen . <p> We know what it feels like when someone says , " You handled that meeting with so much grace . " " I noticed how patient you were with your kid just now . " Those moments linger , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ being enough . Complimenting a stranger , when done thoughtfully , is a small rebellion against the invisibility so many of us feel daily . <p> The One-Minute Experiment <p> For one week , offer one sincere compliment a day to someone you do n't know well . Skip the generic flattery and the commentary on someone 's body . What you 're going for is genuine noticing , something specific that you actually saw and appreciated . <p> " I just wanted to say , you explained that so clearly . " " The way you handled that customer was really kind . " " I love your phone case , that pattern is so fun ! " <p> Authenticity and specificity are the keys to this experiment . Research on effective praise shows that concrete , behavior-based feedback feels more credible and more meaningful than vague ( or even worse , insincere ) positivity . When you name what you are noticing , you communicate that you were actually paying attention , and paying attention to others in today 's world is rare . <p> What It Changes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that this little experiment makes you more observant . You start scanning your environment not for what is wrong , but for what is worth appreciating . That shift alone can change the tone of your day . <p> Barbara Fredrickson 's broaden-and-build theory ( 2001 ) suggests that positive emotions expand our thinking and help us build social resources over time . When you look for moments to affirm , you are training your brain to widen rather than narrow , building connection rather than guarding against it . <p> You also practice tolerating mild awkwardness . The first few compliments might feel clumsy , and honestly , that 's okay . That 's how most growth starts . With repetition , it becomes more natural , and most people , it turns out , are relieved when someone is simply kind . <p> There 's a quieter shift that happens , too . When you practice offering appreciation outward , you often soften inward as well . It becomes harder to be relentlessly critical of yourself when you spend your days noticing what is good in others . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be easy to dismiss all this as small , inconsequential actions . A boot compliment is not going to solve systemic injustice or climate change . Culture is shaped in micro-moments like this , however , and norms shift through repetition . When we choose to notice and name what is good , we create tiny pockets of psychological safety . We make it a little more acceptable to smile at someone in line , a little more normal to say , " I see you , and I value you . " <p> And it 's important to also remember that you do n't get to see most of the ripple effects you create . The woman in the yellow boots might carry that comment into her next conversation , walk into her meeting standing a little taller , or maybe tell a friend later about the stranger who loved her boots . You 'll never know , and guess what -- that does n't mean it did n't matter . <p> A Word on Not Being Weird About It <p> This little experiment does come with a caveat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ You can feel when someone is open to a moment of connection and when they 'd rather be left alone , and it 's worth trusting that instinct . A quick , respectful comment and then moving on is almost always enough . An authentic compliment like this is a gift of attention , and the best gifts do n't ask for anything back . <p> Try It Today <p> On your next errand or walk through the office , look up . Find one person and one thing about them that is genuinely worth naming , and say it . It will take less than a minute , and it might surprise you how much it shifts the air between you . If you are like me , you will walk away feeling a little more awake because you participated in making the world slightly warmer . <p> Joy does n't have to be a grand event . Sometimes it 's simply noticing a pair of yellow boots and having the courage to say so . <p> References <p> Fredrickson , B. L. ( 2001 ) . The role @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of positive emotions . American Psychologist , 56(3) , 218 -- 226.

@@134338795 <p> Is artificial intelligence the salvation of mankind , or its downfall ? Are markets justified in bidding up AI stocks as high as they have , or is it all a bubble ? Will we look back on the hundreds of billions of dollars the AI titans are currently investing in capacity as having laid the foundations for a new age of prosperity , or as an especially destructive example of the herd instinct , this time among tech billionaires ? <p> At the moment , the best answer to questions like these is : Yes . Nobody knows anything , but everyone is certain about everything . Oceans of hype wash across social media , whether hailing the coming revolution or bewailing it , sometimes written by the same people . <p> There is one thing , however , on which there is widespread , if not universal agreement : AI will lead to massive , extinction-event-level loss of jobs , especially in the knowledge economy -- precisely the university-educated , service-industry , symbolic-analyst professions that were supposed to inherit the Earth , insulated from the fluctuations of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ them . In the more extreme formulations , AI will kill every kind of job , not only the virtual but the physical as well -- a world , literally , without work . AI will be smarter than we are , quicker , stronger -- better at everything , at a fraction of the cost , without need of vacation , rest or employee health benefits . It will create great wealth for those who control it -- for as long as they do -- but will cost everyone else their livelihoods , and as important , a sense of purpose . Society will be consumed with redistributing income ; individuals , with finding meaning in their lives . <p> And it will all happen so fast ! This is the other thing on which there is widespread agreement . The world might have endured previous industrial revolutions , but they were neither so universal -- every job made obsolete , not just some -- nor so instantaneous : millions upon millions laid off , more or less at the same time . Even if an answer to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the short run will be so painful , and costly , as to be overwhelming . <p> Mind you , there 's very little evidence of this happening , as yet . Unemployment across the OECD remains at about 5 per cent , where it has been for the last three years -- and lower than at any time in the previous two decades . Still , there are reports , anecdotes , warning signs : a big law firm laying off hundreds of support staff here , a chemicals giant there . <p> The past couple of weeks have seemed especially portentous , with the release of upgraded versions of the two leading AI chatbots , OpenAI 's ChatGPT and Anthropic 's Claude , together with variants dedicated to writing computer code ( called , respectively , Codex and Claude Code ) . Indeed , OpenAI boasts that its latest update was itself written largely by AI : The model , it says , " was instrumental in creating itself . " The news caused a massive selloff in software stocks , similar to those that have hit the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sectors . <p> The situation has been likened to the eerie sense of disquiet we all felt in the early weeks of 2020 : First you heard about those people falling ill with some mysterious disease in China , then you thought maybe you should cancel that trip to Europe , the next moment we were up to our ears in it . So why wait till more evidence comes in now ? No one likes to be caught unaware , or to be accused of complacency . And besides , there can be a certain , shall we say , convenience to it . A firm that is laying off a fifth of its staff firm may find it easier to attribute it to " getting ahead of the AI curve " than to declining demand for its product -- or the mistakes of management . <p> There are benefits to playing Cassandra , not least to people in the AI business themselves , who have taken to issuing ever direr warnings of the potentially apocalyptic effects of their wares , even as they are developing them at full @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ display a fetching concern for the public good , but it 's a great way to advertise the power of your product -- in the tradition of those movie posters warning " Not suitable for the faint of heart ! " <p> Let 's leave the broader fears about AI -- everything from how it might be used by terrorists or other bad actors , to the potential for catastrophe in seemingly innocent prompts ( the quickest way to " find a solution for climate change " might be to eliminate humanity ) , all the way to the full-on , **26;87;TOOLONG , superintelligence nightmare scenarios -- to one side for the moment : Not because they 're not serious , but because they 're so unknowable . <p> But what about the mass unemployment storyline ? Should we be preparing for that particular disaster ? Are we really likely to see , as claimed , half of all entry-level white-collar jobs wiped out within five years ? A global job market collapse by next year ? A future in which " no one will work " ? <p> Anything @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of reasons to doubt it . There will obviously be some jobs lost , possibly a great many , in certain sectors . But the number of jobs lost may not be anything like what has been imagined , and they may well be offset by the numbers of jobs created -- not just in the long term , but even in the short . <p> We should be aware , first , of the assumptions embedded in the typical disaster scenario . It assumes , first , that AI continues on the kind of exponential curve of improvement on which it has seemed to be until now -- or even accelerates , as the idea of AI building itself suggests . There are knowledgeable people who contest this , arguing that the gains from scale have already been exhausted ( you can only download the entire internet once ) and the gains from algorithmic improvement are harder to extract . <p> Second , it assumes that companies are quick to invest in AI , and quick to find ways to capitalize on their investment . History suggests that is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and ways of doing things , until they absolutely have to . The old technologies are proven ; the new are uncertain . It 's costly , disruptive and risky . Even after they have made the jump to a new technology , it often takes a long time to figure out how to use it to full advantage . It took years before electrification produced widespread productivity gains ; the same applied to computers , or the internet . <p> But all right , presumably the layoffs follow , eventually , as AI is fully phased in . Why should we believe these will not be as calamitous as feared ? The simplest reason -- and the one that has been observed in every previous wave of technological change -- is rooted in the productivity gains to which the introduction of AI , and the jobs it eliminates , gives rise . <p> Higher productivity means lower costs ; lower costs lead to lower prices ; lower prices ( along with higher wages , which tend to track productivity ) mean higher real incomes ; higher real incomes can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ industries . Which things ? What industries ? Who knows -- but there 's never any shortage of things for people to spend their money on . Consumer wants are limitless , as is the ingenuity of entrepreneurs in filling those wants . Who knew they needed an iPhone 20 years ago ? <p> But AI will be better than us at everything ! Surely this time is different : The job loss , surely , will be across the board , rather than sectoral . Not necessarily . AI 's technological advances may not cost workers their jobs , but enhance them , allowing each to produce more with the same effort . If each worker is more productive with AI , it does n't automatically follow that a company will try to produce the same amount with fewer workers : It may try to get its existing work force to produce more . It may even -- stay with me here -- hire more workers . <p> The phenomenon is known as the " Jevons paradox , " after the eminent 19th-century British economist William Stanley Jevons . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ use of coal . And yet , he noticed , this had not led to a reduction in total coal consumption , as had been assumed , but rather to an increase in it . Why ? Because as steam power became cheaper , people found new uses for it that would have been beyond their reach before . <p> The same has been observed in all sorts of modern settings . Perhaps the most famous example : The advent of the spreadsheet app did not eliminate the need for accountants . Rather , it made them capable of doing all sorts of tasks they could not have done previously . <p> Before , they were employed keeping track of columns of numbers on paper ledgers ; any change to one required hours of labour to update the rest . After , they could perform much more sophisticated forecasts and complex financial analysis . <p> And not just for the sort of large corporation that might have been able to afford such things in the past , but for small businesses as well . Result : Total employment in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other reasons to believe that human labour will survive the advent of AI . One is a kind of comparative-advantage argument : Even if AI is better than we are at everything , in absolute terms , it will still pay for it to specialize in the things that it is " most best " at , and leave the rest to us . Or to combine our efforts , in ways that best harness the relative strengths of each . <p> Another is simply that we have a particular interest in our own species . It has been 30 years since a computer first beat the greatest living human chess player . Yet the marquee event in chess is still between two unaided humans ; competitions between computers remain curiosities . Likewise , we still want to watch a field of humans in the 100-metre dash , notwithstanding the invention of the automobile . While we also watch humans racing in cars , will we be as interested in watching a race between driverless cars ? I doubt it . <p> We 've had machines that can make everything @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and are willing to pay for , things that have been " made by hand , " whether a piece of furniture , an article of clothing , or a meal . The camera did not eliminate painting , nor did the movies kill the theatre . So long as humans survive AI , so will human labour . I think . 
@@134338798 <h> Data Dive with Nik Nanos : Canadians are clamouring for a stronger military <p> Members of the Canadian Armed Forces march during a Remembrance Day ceremony in Montreal on Nov. 11 , 2025 . A recent poll shows Canadians ' historic self-image as peacekeepers is clashing with the reality of a changing , more dangerous world.Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press <p> Nik Nanos is the chief data scientist at Nanos Research , an executive fellow at the School of Public Policy at the University of Calgary , and the official pollster for The Globe and Mail and CTV News . <p> Canada is witnessing a once-in-a-generation shift in opinion on matters of national defence . In the absence of a traditional war , a wartime mentality is emerging : Canadians have an appetite for more defence spending as they see significant global threats . <p> A study commissioned by the University of Calgary and completed by Nanos Research in late 2025 points to a series of historic shifts that will influence both Canada 's defence posture and strategy . U.S. President Donald Trump 's musings about Canada becoming the 51st @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Just as many Canadians agree that the best way for Canada to be a world leader in foreign affairs is to build international consensus ( 66 per cent agree with this statement ) as believe that Canada needs a strong military to be effective in international relations ( 65 per cent agree with this statement ) . <p> When asked how Canada can best advance its place in the world , trade topped the list ( 91 per cent of respondents felt it was important ) , followed by diplomacy ( 83 per cent ) , national defence ( 71 per cent ) , environment ( 63 per cent ) , foreign aid ( 51 per cent ) and immigration ( 41 per cent ) . Since the benchmark study was conducted in 2020 , the importance of trade and defence are up nine and 17 points respectively , while environment and immigration have decreased in importance 16 and 19 points respectively . <p> Right now public sentiment suggests that Canada 's strategy should be driven by trade and defence , and enabled by diplomacy . <p> Prime Minister Mark @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Davos , on the new relationship between great and middle powers , points to a pivot . Only time will tell whether this is a rupture or a transition . <p> The short-term polling suggests the former . The belief that Canada faces international threats has surged from 41 per cent in 2020 to 58 per cent in 2025 . <p> When it comes to specific threats , foreign interference and disinformation was cited by more than eight in 10 Canadians ( 82 per cent ) , followed by the U.S. ( 71 per cent ) , Russia ( 61 per cent ) , climate change ( 60 per cent ) and China ( 56 per cent ) . <p> When it comes to defence , 30 per cent of Canadians still see their country 's role as that of a peacekeeper and mediator , and 65 per cent say Canada needs a strong military for effective international relations . This speaks to the collision of our historic self-image as peacekeepers with the reality of a changing , more dangerous world . <p> A majority of Canadians ( 57 per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Atlantic Treaty Organization ( NATO ) military conflict with Russia , Canada should support NATO militarily . In contrast , a mere 13 per cent of Canadians would support the U.S. militarily in a conflict with China while 29 per cent say they would oppose the conflict and urge diplomatic solutions . <p> In a world of changing threat perceptions , the appetite for defence spending has increased from 41 per cent in 2020 to 62 per cent . But even with the increased appetite for defence spending , views on the Canadian Armed Forces remain mixed . When asked about how much confidence Canadians have in the ability of CAF leaders to shape policies that benefit Canada , 38 per cent ( and only 31 per cent of Canadians under the age of 35 ) say they have confidence , down from 43 per cent in 2020 . This ranks below academia ( 44 per cent of Canadians have confidence ) and intelligence agencies ( 43 per cent ) , but above the defence industry ( 27 per cent ) , politicians ( 24 per cent ) and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an open-ended question where they could say anything in terms of what comes to mind when they think of the Canadian Armed Forces , the lack of resources tops the list , with that responsetripling over the past five years from 6 to 21 per cent . References to the CAF being weak or ineffective is up by a multiple of five , from three to 16 per cent , while peacekeeping is down from 21 to 11 per cent . Canadians also associated the CAF with small size ( 7 per cent ) , being well-trained ( 6 per cent ) , having old or outdated equipment ( 5 per cent ) , protection or providing security ( 5 per cent ) , bravery ( 3 per cent ) , and patriotism ( 3 per cent ) . Of note , one in 50 Canadians ( 2 per cent ) associate a culture of harassment with the CAF -- up from 1 per cent in 2020 . <p> This suggests Canadians view the CAF as a small , underfunded , but well-trained organization that has difficulty being effective because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are much more likely to think that the priority when buying military equipment should be creating jobs ( 64 per cent ) rather than getting the best price ( 7 per cent ) . Asked separately how much of a priority buying military equipment from the United States should be , only 12 per cent of Canadians agreed buying American should be a priority . <p> When it comes to the Canadian Armed Forces , there are a number of bright spots . Canadians are more than seven times more likely to have a positive impression ( 68 per cent ) than a negative ( 9 per cent ) one if a friend or family member decided to join the CAF . They are six times more likely to think the CAF is good at what it does ( 56 per cent ) rather than not good ( 9 per cent ) . <p> It also appears many Canadians are willing to personally serve their country in different capacities were Canada to be involved in a major conflict . Fifty-seven per cent report an interest in volunteering to support civil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ join a civil defence organization on a part-time ( 45 per cent ) or full-time ( 32 per cent ) basis . Significantly , nearly one in five Canadians ( 19 per cent ) say they would be open to joining the Forces as a part-time job ( as in reserve duty ) and 12 per cent would join the CAF as a full-time job ( or enlist ) . <p> Canadians are living in a moment where they feel the ground shifting , recalibrating long-standing assumptions about allies , threats , and our own military capacity . Past complacency is gone . The appetite for action on defence investments is strengthening . More importantly , faced with a major challenge , many Canadians are ready to serve .
